title: Duplicate criterion left undefined
reviewer_explanation: The brief's phrase 'look the same' is copied without defining which fields must match or how closely. The requirement cannot be built or tested consistently. Record this as an open question for the visitor rather than restating it as a requirement.
passage: REQ-2: Two claims are duplicates when they look the same. Use no other duplicate rule.
builder_note: REQ-2 defines 'look the same' as an exact match on patientRef, serviceDate, procedureCode and amount, and labels this as an assumption the visitor must confirm. REQ-5 records near-matches as an open question.

title: AC-1 silently invents exact-match rule
reviewer_explanation: AC-1 treats 'look the same' as all five fields being identical, including claimId. That is a second rule, which REQ-2 forbids. It also means resubmitted claims with new claimIds would never be flagged. State the assumption explicitly or ask the visitor.
passage: a second claim with those same five values. They look the same, so flag both for review.
builder_note: The exact-match rule is now stated as an explicit assumption. claimId is excluded from the comparison, and AC-1 shows that two claims with different claimIds are still flagged, so resubmitted claims are caught.

title: AC-2 changes two fields
reviewer_explanation: The non-match claim differs in claimId (2 vs 1) as well as amount, yet only amount is named as the reason. Varying a single field would make the test show clearly which difference prevents the flag.
passage: amount 80 is not amount 100, so they do not look the same and are not flagged.
builder_note: AC-2 now differs only in amount among the compared fields. claimId is not compared, so its difference does not affect the result.

title: Rounding method not specified
reviewer_explanation: REQ-4 does not say how halves are rounded. A result such as 70.25 could become 70.3 (half up) or 70.2 (banker's rounding). The brief is silent, so this could be flagged as an open question.
passage: REQ-4: Round the final grade to 1 decimal place.
builder_note: REQ-4 now flags half-rounding (70.25 to 70.3 or 70.2) as an open question for the requester.

title: No test for under-four homework
reviewer_explanation: No acceptance criterion checks that nothing is dropped when homework has fewer than 4 scores, or exactly which score is dropped when the lowest is tied. Adding one would confirm the threshold in REQ-2.
passage: REQ-2: If homework has 4 or more scores, drop the lowest score before averaging
builder_note: AC-2 covers 3 homework scores with no drop (average 80, final 68.5). REQ-2 now says only one of tied lowest scores is dropped; the result is the same whichever copy is removed.

title: Rounding lacks acceptance criterion
reviewer_explanation: Both examples already land on one decimal, so no criterion actually tests REQ-4. An example that needs rounding would confirm the behavior.
passage: AC-2: With no quiz scores, the quiz category is 0, so the same homework and exam give 0.2*90 + 0.3*0 + 0.5*60 = 48.0.
builder_note: AC-4 needs rounding: 16.333 + 21.15 + 38.5 = 75.983, shown as 76.0.

title: Empty exam is not zero
reviewer_explanation: REQ-3 requires a category with no scores to count as 0. This line uses exam[0] whenever the exam array is present. An empty array is present, so exam[0] is undefined, not 0, and the final grade is wrong whenever there is no exam.
builder_note: examScore now uses exam.length > 0 ? exam[0] : 0, so an empty exam counts as 0 under REQ-3. Added an empty-exam test: 18 + 22.5 + 0 = 40.5.

title: Multiple or longer streaks undefined
reviewer_explanation: The requirements do not say what to return if the list holds two separate runs of 3 or more absences. They also do not say whether a 4th or later consecutive absence alerts the counsellor again. The brief implies a single date. Specify the first date reached, or every date, and when alerts repeat.
passage: When absences reach 3 in a row, tell a counsellor and return the date the streak reached 3; otherwise return nothing.
builder_note: REQ-4 now states only the first date a streak reached 3 is returned, with no repeat alert for a 4th+ absence or a later streak, flagged as an assumption; AC-3 and AC-4 test this.

title: AC-3 wording overly broad
reviewer_explanation: Read literally, AC-3 says any short run returns nothing, even when a separate run of 3 exists elsewhere in the same input. Reword it as: input with no run of 3 or more consecutive absences returns nothing.
passage: AC-3: Any run of fewer than 3 absences returns nothing.
builder_note: Replaced with AC-5: empty input or input with no run of 3 or more consecutive absences returns nothing.

title: Count reset prevents any streak
reviewer_explanation: Written as a separate sentence after the count-is-3 check, Otherwise sets count to 0 whenever the count is not 3. The first and second absences are cleared, so the count never reaches 3 and AC-1, AC-3 and AC-4 fail.
builder_note: The reset is now tied only to status "present". An absent day adds 1 and returns at 3, so the trace gives 1, 2, 3 and Monday for AC-1. AC-3 and AC-4 now pass, and AC-2 still resets.

title: False confirmation of free-unit rule
reviewer_explanation: AC-3 says equal totals for 7 and 8 units confirm that the free unit must already be on the line. That equality only follows from the unconfirmed floor(units/4) assumption in REQ-2. It does not establish the rule.
passage: This is the same as 8 units, which confirms the 4th unit must be on the line to be free.
builder_note: AC-3 no longer claims that the equal totals confirm the free-unit rule. It now says the result follows from the REQ-2 assumption and is not evidence for it.

title: No rounding rule for discount
reviewer_explanation: Taking 10% off can produce fractions of a cent, for example 0.045 for one unit at 0.05. The draft does not say when to round, to how many decimals, or how. Different implementations could then return different line totals.
passage: apply 10% to the paid amount and return that figure as the line total
builder_note: REQ-1 sets one rounding step at the end, to 2 decimals, assuming half-up pending confirmation. AC-5 tests the 0.045 case and expects 0.05.

title: No leftover or small-quantity criteria
reviewer_explanation: AC-1 only tests a multiple of four. Add criteria for leftover units, for example 7 units at 5.00: 1 free, 6 paid, 30.00, total 27.00. Also add one for fewer than four units and one for zero or invalid units.
builder_note: Added criteria for leftover units (AC-3, 7 units gives 27.00), for fewer than four units (AC-2, 3 units gives 13.50), and for zero and invalid units (AC-4).

stage: Requirements: final check of the merged document
title: Example skips discount math
reviewer_explanation: One unit at 0.05 has a normal price of 0.05, not 0.045. The value 0.045 appears only after the 10 percent discount (0.05 x 0.90). The example states a wrong figure for those inputs.
passage: For example, 1 unit at 0.05 gives 0.045, which rounds to 0.05.
builder_note: Real issue: the REQ-1 example went from 1 unit at 0.05 straight to 0.045 and skipped the discount step. It now gives the normal price of 0.05, then shows the 10% discount (0.05 x 0.90 = 0.045) before rounding to 0.05. The final result was already correct, and it matches AC-5, so P0 overstates the severity. Nothing else was changed.

title: Floating-point failure claim wrong
reviewer_explanation: Binary 0.05 times 0.90 is slightly above 0.045, not 0.0449999..., so half-up still gives 0.05 and does not fail AC-5. Avoiding binary floating point is still sound, but this sentence states a wrong result.
builder_note: Removed the wrong claim. Binary 0.05 x 0.90 is about 0.045000000000000005, which still rounds to 0.05. The arithmetic line now gives a correct example of a float failing half-up: 1.005 is stored as 1.00499999... and rounds to 1.00. The scaled-integer approach and the AC-5 cents example are unchanged.

title: Line total conversion throws
reviewer_explanation: whole is a BigInt, and BigInt plus a string throws TypeError in JavaScript. Every valid line, including AC-1 through AC-5, crashes here and never returns lineTotal.
builder_note: BigInt + string does not throw in JavaScript; the BigInt is converted to its string form and concatenated. Only mixing BigInt with Number in arithmetic throws TypeError. For AC-1, cents = 2700n, so whole + '.' + rest gives "27.00" and Number(...) gives 27. AC-5 traced: num = 1*5*9*100 = 4500, den = 100*10 = 1000, q = 4, r = 500, so it rounds half-up to 5 cents, giving 0.05. AC-2 (13.50), AC-3 (27.00) and AC-4 (0.00) also hold. Code is unchanged apart from a clarifying comment.

title: Epsilon can mis-round cents
reviewer_explanation: Adding an epsilon before rounding can move a result just below a half-cent boundary onto that boundary and change interest by one cent. That breaks round-to-2-decimals for ordinary inputs, not only float noise. Round the true quotient with no epsilon nudge.
builder_note: Removed the epsilon. round2 now rounds the computed quotient directly to the nearest cent.

title: Unconfirmed half rounding shipped
reviewer_explanation: The contract says the exact-half method waits on REQ-4, and REQ-4 says it still needs confirming. Choosing half away from zero ships an unconfirmed rule. The given examples are not exact halves, so they do not prove this choice. Hold it as with REQ-5.
builder_note: Dropped half away from zero. The exact-half rule is a marked stub held for REQ-4, like the REQ-5 items, and exact-half tests are deferred.

title: Repeat and no-alert behaviour undefined
reviewer_explanation: The requirements do not say whether only the first triggering payment is returned or every later payment in the same window also alerts, nor what is returned when no alert occurs. These are open questions for the visitor, not facts to invent, but they should be resolved before approval.
passage: REQ-4: Return the time of the payment that caused the alert.
builder_note: REQ-4 states that no alert is raised when no payment makes a 6th in one period. Whether later payments raise further alerts is recorded as an open question for the requester rather than invented, and it must be answered before approval.

title: AC-2 lacks observable outcome
reviewer_explanation: AC-2 restates the boundary rule but gives no expected system result, so it cannot be tested directly. It could be tied to an alert or no-alert outcome, using only the stated facts, for example by building a case on the AC-1 sequence.
passage: AC-2: Payments at 10:00 and 10:10 are not in the same period.
builder_note: B's AC-2 and A's matching AC-4 are replaced by a testable case built on the AC-1 sequence. With 10:10 in place of 10:09 the expected result is no alert, because 10:00 and 10:10 are in different periods and the period ending at 10:10 holds only 5 payments.

title: Stated quotient is wrong
reviewer_explanation: 100 divided by 48 equals 2.0833..., not 2.08. The ceiling is still 3, so the pallet count is right, but the equality states a wrong figure.
builder_note: The quotient is now written as 100 / 48 = 2.083..., which still rounds up to 3.

title: Example blamed on brief
reviewer_explanation: The brief states only the 48-carton and 1000 kg limits and rounding up. The answer of 2 is a made-up fact to check, not a brief example. The correction to 3 is right; the source name is not.
passage: The brief's example answer of 2 is wrong
builder_note: The 2-pallet answer is now credited to the made-up example, not the brief.

title: Weight rule ignores indivisible cartons
reviewer_explanation: Cartons cannot be split across pallets. With 5 cartons of 400 kg, total 2000/1000 gives 2, but each pallet fits only 2 cartons (800 kg), so 3 pallets are needed. Use per-pallet capacity min(48, floor(1000/weight)), then round up count divided by that.
passage: Take carton count divided by 48 and total kg divided by 1000, round each up, and return the greater whole number.
builder_note: Draft B's total-weight rule is replaced by c = min(48, floor(1000 / w)) and ceil(n / c). AC-3 checks 5 cartons at 400 kg, which gives 3 pallets.

title: Edge and invalid inputs unspecified
reviewer_explanation: There is no requirement for zero cartons, zero or negative weight, or a single carton over 1000 kg, which can never be palletised. Behaviour for these inputs should be defined before approval.
passage: Given a carton count and one weight shared by every carton, return how many pallets are needed.
builder_note: REQ-5 and AC-5 now define the result for zero cartons, a zero or negative weight, a carton over 1000 kg and invalid inputs.

title: Example misattributed to brief
reviewer_explanation: The 2-pallet answer comes from the made-up example in the facts, not from the brief. The correction itself is right; only the attribution is wrong.
passage: The brief answer of 2 is wrong
builder_note: The 2-pallet answer is attributed to the made-up example in the facts.

stage: Requirements: final check of the merged document
title: Zero carton count contradiction
reviewer_explanation: REQ-5 rejects zero carton counts with an error. REQ-1 allows n of zero or more, REQ-4 returns 0 when n is 0, and AC-5 expects 0 pallets for 0 cartons at 8 kg. One of these rules is wrong and they cannot be implemented together.
passage: Zero, negative, non-whole carton counts and non-numeric inputs are also rejected with an error.
builder_note: The finding is correct. REQ-5 rejected zero carton counts, but REQ-1, REQ-4 and AC-5 all allow n = 0 and expect 0 pallets. I removed zero counts from the REQ-5 rejection list. REQ-5 now rejects negative or non-whole counts. In the same sentence, it states that weights of 0 kg or less are rejected. This keeps REQ-5 consistent with REQ-1 (w > 0) and with the AC-5 error for a weight of 0 kg. Nothing else was changed.

title: Float floor overloads pallet
reviewer_explanation: For the next double above 1000/9, 1000/w rounds to 9, so c is 9, but nine cartons weigh 1000+2^-45 kg. The guard only adds a carton when a float product looks legal, and never reduces an overweight c. That breaks the 1000 kg cap.
builder_note: The old guard could only raise c. c is now corrected both ways with an exact c * w <= 1000 test (error-free product), so a float floor can never overload a pallet. A test for the double just above 1000/9 is added.

title: Open point reopens settled case
reviewer_explanation: AC-1 already requires 3 pallets for 100 cartons at 8 kg and says 2 is wrong because 2 pallets hold at most 96. Line 5 agrees. Asking the requester to confirm 3 can still overturn a closed rule and fail AC-1.
builder_note: The open point is removed. AC-1 already settles 3 pallets, and the requester cannot reopen it.

title: Infinity uses wrong error
reviewer_explanation: A weight greater than 1000 must throw carton too heavy for a pallet. Infinity is a number greater than 1000, so that message applies. The finite check rejects it first as invalid cartonWeightKg, which breaks the contract's error split.
builder_note: The finite check is dropped. Only non-numbers, NaN and weights of 0 or less are "invalid cartonWeightKg". Infinity is above 1000, so it gets "carton too heavy for a pallet", and a test is added.
